S o, did you invest in the market-leading company that has warned its technology could ultimately help destroy humanity?
You could have put a gun to my head and I still wouldn’t have signed up for shares in Anthropic , the artificial intelligence giant behind AI assistant Claude, that warned artificial intelligence could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" in documents accompanying its blockbuster stock market flotation .
To me, it felt a bit like Sarah Connor, heroine of the Terminator films, opening the financial pages to discover that Skynet is floating on Wall Street. Our robots might wipe out humanity… but they make awesome work colleagues!
But if you signed up, you may be disappointed with your allocation.
The shares were in demand among big boys at moneybags institutions. Even a company the size of Anthropic, with the degree of control held by the founders (the big seven newly minted multi-billionaires have 50.1 per cent under its somewhat controversial governance structure), has to keep them sweet.
The small fry - so you and me - could apply for as little as £250 via Hargreaves Lansdown and other platforms. Even if you get only a limited number, this democratisation of the stock market is a welcome development. Why should the big institutions have all the fun? But just because you can buy something doesn't mean you should.
We’re about to find out whether the market’s recent bout of AI nervousness holds true. The reported institutional demand is encouraging for the company. But will that remain the case over the next few days, once the shares start trading and find a level?
I confess Anthropic had already put me off, with its relentlessly irritating podcast advertising. One featured breathless workers discussing their awesome new colleague, Claude , as though he were the office heartthrob. But my reservations go considerably deeper than its marketing department.
It is undeniably a remarkable business. Its annualised revenue reportedly reached $81bn in October. That's phenomenal growth for a company founded just five years ago.
Unfortunately, the numbers on the other side of the ledger are equally extraordinary. Anthropic has computing commitments approaching $900bn. Building the AI revolution requires astonishing quantities of expensive infrastructure, energy and processing power.
And nobody can confidently predict how much profit all this spending will ultimately generate.
That's the problem with a trillion-dollar valuation. Investors aren't simply betting that AI will transform the world. They're betting that Anthropic will capture enough of that transformation to justify its enormous price tag. Those are two very different propositions.
There's another intriguing wrinkle. Some critics suspect the AI giants’ enthusiasm for warnings about existential risk also serves their commercial interests.
Regulation can be a wonderful thing when you're already established. Compliance is expensive. Smaller competitors, perhaps a few Stanford dropouts working on the next technological revolution in an outrageously overpriced San Francisco bedsit, might struggle to afford it.
That doesn't mean Anthropic's safety concerns are insincere. But regulation that protects humanity could also protect the industry's incumbents from competition.
And competition, rather than Claude listening to Guns N' Roses' Appetite for Destruction and getting ideas, may prove the more immediate threat to shareholders.
An investment professional I spoke to wouldn't touch these valuations . The concern isn't whether AI has a future; of course it does. It's whether investors are paying so much for that future that even spectacular success might disappoint them.
Remember: technology changes quickly. Today's cuddly, indispensable AI assistant could become tomorrow's obsolete software . In five years, Anthropic's business might look unrecognisable. Or it may just find itself struggling to keep up.
That’s the risk taken by those who took a punt. They might make a fortune. They should do okay if Anthropic emerges as one of the AI winners. But even that’s a big if.
No one should confuse buying into the future with buying a good investment. Remember: even if Anthropic’s AI bots don't destroy humanity, there's nothing stopping them from destroying your savings. Here endeth the lesson. Now let’s sit back and watch that share price. Good luck!

articles.title_orig: UN climate talks break down without an overarching agreement
articles.title_zh: UN climate talks break down without an overarching agreement
articles.content_orig:
EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels
Cop31 live blog: longest climate summit ever faces collapse
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey .
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.
The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that campaigners have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”
Many countries, including the EU, UK and many developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be the “cover decision”, or main outcome, of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.
Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations.
after newsletter promotion
Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.
For many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis. Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, while African ministers made a dramatic intervention on Friday saying: “We did not come here to beg.”
Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, summed up the view of many on Friday when he said: “The Cop presidents want to tell us this has been a great Cop. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst Cop ever.”
On Sunday, he added: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create.... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”
While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño , the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.
“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

articles.title_orig: China-linked hackers used AI agents to exploit a MONAI Label zero-day, Amazon says
articles.title_zh: China-linked hackers used AI agents to exploit a MONAI Label zero-day, Amazon says
articles.content_orig:
MONAI Label, an open-source server for labelling medical scans, had no patched release when Amazon went public. Maintainers merged a source fix on October 19, but the vulnerable default version is still the only one available, with authentication off by default.
The hospital-software scare is smaller than the viral version, but the speed isn't: Amazon says AI agents went from probing a medical imaging tool to writing files on the server in about 11 minutes. If you ship open-source software with the login switched off by default, that's your timeline now.
Amazon Threat Intelligence says a China-linked operator used autonomous AI agents to find and exploit a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models, according to SecurityWeek and The Hacker News, which both reported on the findings this week. The campaign ran for about 48 hours in September, so what's new this week is the disclosure, not the attack.
It's worth being exact about what was hit, because the aggregator digests going around blurred it. The targets were IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China, not hospitals, and there's no public report of patient records being touched. MONAI Label is research tooling that sits close to clinical work, which is why the story spread, but nothing published so far shows a hospital system was breached. The size of the compromise beyond the university servers hasn't been disclosed.
The flaw is a path traversal bug in the file upload function. According to The Hacker News, it lets someone with no account write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup. Authentication is off by default, which SecurityWeek flagged as part of why the bug was so easy to reach.
Amazon's account is specific about the pace. In its words, quoted by SecurityWeek, "in about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application's API to arbitrarily writing files." The operators then got root by planting Python startup files that ran when a training process started, a reverse shell included. The human set the goal, which was shell access, and picked the targets. The agents chose the method.
Google's threat team named Artex, Cairn, HexStrike AI and PentAGI in a new report, while the FBI says Artex campaigns have hit at least ten sectors, including South Korean banks and ConnectWise customers. More than 1,600 control consoles sat exposed online in early November. - FBI warning about Artex AI hacking tools - AI agents breaking into networks within hours
Amazon says it has high confidence this was a true zero-day, because it found no matching fix, issue, advisory or earlier mention in vulnerability databases for the project. The Hacker News identified the agent framework as Cairn, an open-source attack tool. The tool isn't new. The operator and the target are.
On attribution, Amazon is cautious. It ties the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, citing Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings and targets likely to interest China. No named group has been attached to it.
This is where it gets uncomfortable for anyone who maintains software. According to The Hacker News, the MONAI Label maintainers merged a source fix on October 19, but no patched release exists yet, and the advisory lists no available update. SecurityWeek reports the developers published their advisory this week, rate the bug critical, and say the fix will ship in the next release. So a fix has been sitting in the code for more than a month while the vulnerable default version is the only one you can download.
Frankly, that gap is the story. MONAI Label is a volunteer-scale open-source project, not a vendor with a legal team and a patch cadence, and nobody can sensibly sue it. The institutions running it carry the risk, and most won't be watching a GitHub commit log. If an agent can map an API and land a file write in the time it takes to make a coffee, a month between fix and release is a long time to leave the front door open.
It also fits a pattern that healthcare security teams have been warning about. The FBI and Google warned earlier this month, as the American Hospital Association relayed on November 16, that attackers are using agentic AI platforms to move from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours in some intrusions. Amazon's case stands out because the agents found the bug themselves rather than exploiting a known one.
For now, the practical advice is plain. If you run MONAI Label, turn authentication on, keep it off the public internet, and build from the October 19 source fix rather than waiting. If you sell software into hospitals or universities, assume your default settings will be probed by something that doesn't sleep.
Neither the MONAI Label maintainers nor Amazon has said how many servers were compromised, and no patched release has been scheduled.
Researcher Eaton Zveare says CreditNirvana, owned by Perfios, left Aditya Birla Capital Finance call recordings and borrower files open through a hardcoded API key and a skipped token check. The vendor patched both bugs on June 2, but no one has said whether borrowers were told. - CreditNirvana vulnerabilities exposed 6.6 million accounts - CreditNirvana AI debt collection security flaws

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship still on fire off Finland after attack
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship still on fire off Finland after attack
articles.content_orig:
A fire on board a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones off the coast of Finland in the Baltic Sea continued to burn through the night even as efforts were made to douse the flames, the Finnish coastguard said.
Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remains at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.
Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.
The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

articles.title_orig: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.title_zh: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.content_orig:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain, as Iran has intensified attacks over the past week, hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and downing US drones.
At least 25 tankers have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, in the past seven days, causing the Gulf oil flow to drop sharply.
The escalating attacks come as Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country is facing what he called a “silent economic war” amid US sanctions and a naval blockade.
So what is behind Iran’s latest escalation, and will it trigger a new round of hostilities between Tehran and Washington or force the two sides to sit down for talks to end the war that has caused a global energy crisis?
Bahrain has faced the brunt of Iran’s attacks in recent days.
On Saturday, Manama said an Iranian strike hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire , as it thwarted several other attacks that day.
The IRGC said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, claiming to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
Iranian state media reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain crashed on Sitra Island near Manama, sparking a large fire.
The IRGC said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Iran has justified the attacks as a response to continued violations of its airspace, including by US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones.
Bahrain has faced three drone attacks in recent days after a lull in fighting for several weeks.
Iran’s army on Saturday said its air defences fired a missile at a US F-16 jet over the Gulf the previous evening, damaging the aircraft, the IRNA news agency reported. However, US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, stating that “all US fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for”.
Iranian forces on Sunday also said they shot down another MQ-1 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC claimed it was the 20th US drone of this type to be shot down since the war began in late February and the fourth in the past 24 hours.
Meanwhile, British maritime authorities reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman.
Al Jazeera correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week, with about 25 since November 14.
Last week, the Iranian army also said it targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base. The attack came after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under effective Iranian control.
Oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz has seen a considerable dip as Iran has escalated attacks on a near-daily basis.
According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), 263 ships passed through the key waterway between November 12 and 18, which is 15 percent fewer than the previous week and 20 percent fewer than the week before that.
Of those vessels, 37 were oil tankers, down from 52 the previous week, UKMTO reported on Friday.
The figures, however, could be higher as vessels passing through as part of shadow fleets are not officially registered.
About 135 ships passed daily through the vital strait before the war began in February.
Last week, the US maritime agency warned that the Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums, with insurance rates up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war to 3.5-7.5 percent.
Oil prices have spiked, crossing $100 a barrel before settling down to $83, still more than $15 from before the war.
Cumulative losses from the conflict have now reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
The IEA, however, added that the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4 percent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response.
As Iran has ramped up attacks, senior officials have asked the US to choose between surrendering to missiles or to diplomacy.
The attacks indicate that Iran is using its leverage in the conflict, sending the message that the US allies in the region will continue to bear the brunt of its actions if the war does not end.
The attacks aim to diminish US military capabilities in the region and “also to spread the pain of the war widely to include the entire [Gulf region] and, indirectly, global economies via higher shipping costs and stressed supplies of essentials”, Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, told Al Jazeera.
The single biggest driver of this strategy, Khouri said, is for Iran to continually ensure that it will no longer “suffer alone from US-Israel-imperial assaults”.
Tehran is hoping to change US policy by revealing its inability to protect its own facilities or those of its Arab allies, which could prompt Arab governments to press US President Donald Trump to end the war, Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, added.
Meanwhile, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that he considers the economic blockade imposed by the US on Iran an act of war.
“We consider the economic siege a hostile act, and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” Gharibabadi told Iranian reporters.
The ongoing US naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and a wave of new sanctions imposed in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast are hurting Iran economically.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran, has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027.
However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure.
The strikes on US interests in the Gulf in recent days have therefore been viewed as a defiant response to the US campaign. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.
Trump may choose to declare victory and walk away from the war on Iran rather than negotiate a deal, but continuing the naval blockade on Iran would risk further military escalation, says Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Parsi said Trump was unlikely to accept an agreement that could be seen in Washington as showing the war had failed.
“If he continues the blockade, there will be escalation,” Parsi warned, arguing that Iran would not refrain from retaliating against continued economic pressure.
He said Trump would need to “slowly, perhaps imperceptibly, lift the blockade, as well as lift some of the sanctions” if he wanted to withdraw from the confrontation without renewed fighting.
Hassan Ahmadian, professor at the University of Tehran, said Iran is forcing a “binary” choice on Trump.
If Washington lets the tankers pass, the US blockade “ends without an agreement or war”, Ahmadian said on X. However, if the US attacks the vessels, it could face “Iranian responses that will be difficult for [Trump] to avoid”.
Trump said on Saturday he had plans to make a deal with Iran that is “permanent” and prevents it from getting a nuclear weapon.
He also told US broadcaster Fox News that he was never very interested in regime change in Iran, but called its new leadership “more rational”.

articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”

articles.title_zh: The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the 5th Time This Century, and History Says It's Obvious What Comes Next for Stocks
articles.content_orig:
By Sean Williams – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:36AM EST
10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›
With less than six weeks left in 2026, investors have little to complain about. The mature-stock-driven Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI -1.93% ) , broad-based S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -3.70% ) , and tech-focused Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -5.28% ) have all catapulted to several record highs this year, driven by the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, better-than-expected corporate earnings, and initial public offering euphoria.
While Wall Street's major stock indexes have made a habit of climbing the proverbial wall of worry and rising over the long term, history also makes clear that bull markets don't last forever. If things seem too perfect for investors, they often are .
Though any number of headwinds can knock the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite off their respective pedestals, one stands out. We're currently witnessing the stock market do something for only the fifth time this century, and history doesn't mince its words about what comes next for stocks.
Image source: Getty Images.
Despite a parabolic move in outstanding margin debt sending all the wrong signals, the biggest worry for Wall Street and investors is premium stock valuations.
To be clear, past events can't guarantee what the future holds. Nevertheless, history has shown a tendency to rhyme on Wall Street more often than not, making it an excellent teaching tool for those investors willing to listen.
Most investors rely on the time-tested price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio when evaluating individual companies or the broader market. While the P/E ratio, which is derived using trailing 12-month earnings per share (EPS), is incredibly useful for quickly sizing up mature businesses, it can lose its utility entirely when recessions occur and EPS turns negative.
For Wall Street's broad-market stock indexes, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio ( CAPE Ratio ), is a far superior valuation tool. The Shiller P/E is based on average inflation-adjusted EPS over the trailing 10 years, meaning recessions won't render it useless.
Though economists introduced the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio less than four decades ago, it's been backtested to January 1871. Over these 156 years, the average reading is a relatively modest 17.45. As of the closing bell on Nov. 17, it was 38.76, or 122% above this long-term average.

What's particularly interesting is how the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite have behaved once the CAPE Ratio surpasses 30, which has happened six times since January 1871, and five times this century, including the present:
On the one hand, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E can't pinpoint when the major stock indexes will peak or which catalyst(s) will send stocks tumbling. But this arbitrary line in the sand has an impeccable track record of foreshadowing significant downturns (20% or greater) in the stock market's major indexes.
History makes it crystal clear that premium valuations aren't sustainable on Wall Street.
Image source: Getty Images.
Sometimes, history doesn't offer the most glowing forecast for the stock market. But altering your perspective can vastly change the projected outcome.
To state what can be an unpleasant truth, stock market corrections, bear markets, and even occasional crashes are normal and healthy events. Given that most of these events are driven by investor emotions, there's not much that can be done from a fiscal or monetary policy perspective to prevent them. Consider these events the cost of admission to take part in one of the world's greatest wealth creators .
But stock market corrections, bear markets, and crashes share an important trait: they're historically short-lived.
The analysts at Bespoke Investment Group examined every S&P 500 bull and bear market since the start of the Great Depression in September 1929, finding a sizable gap between optimism and pessimism on Wall Street.
According to Bespoke's data set, released in late May, the average S&P 500 bear market finds its trough in 286 calendar days (about 9.5 months), while the typical bull market persists for 1,023 calendar days, or nearly 3.6 times as long.
The analysts at Crestmont Research took things even further by examining the rolling 20-year total returns of the benchmark S&P 500 since 1900. Since the S&P wasn't incepted until 1923, this meant tracking the total return of its components in other major indexes back to 1900.
Crestmont's data yielded 107 separate rolling 20-year periods (1900-1919, 1901-1920, and so on, through 2006-2025), all of which generated a positive average annual return .
Hypothetically speaking, since S&P 500-tracking funds didn't exist on U.S. exchanges until January 1993, if an investor had purchased an S&P 500 index fund at any point between 1900 and 2006 and simply held it for 20 years, they would have generated a profit every single time , including dividends. It didn't matter if they bought near a top, before a recession, depression, war, pandemic, or high inflation... the result was always the same.
Even when the stock market gives investors lemons, history says make some lemonade and be patient.

For many car buyers, reliability is about more than avoiding repairs. It’s also about how long a vehicle can remain on the road before it needs to be replaced.
Reaching 250,000 miles (approximately 400,000 km) is a major milestone for drivers hoping to get the most value from their purchase.
This infographic ranks the vehicles with the highest estimated probability of reaching that milestone. The data comes from iSeeCars’ Longest Lasting Cars Study , published in September 2026.
Based on mileage data from more than 395 million vehicles, the study estimates each model’s likelihood of reaching 250,000 miles. It excludes heavy-duty vehicles, models with insufficient data, and vehicles discontinued by 2022.
Toyota’s presence is the clearest pattern in the data, with 10 models making the top 27.
Add five Lexus models, and the two brands account for 15 entries, or approximately 56% of the ranking.
The Lexus LS ranks second at 38.8%, followed by the Toyota 4Runner at 33.1%. Together with the Sequoia, these models give Toyota and Lexus all three top positions.
Toyota’s reputation for reliability is closely linked to its focus on quality control and continuous improvement.
The company’s Toyota Production System emphasizes identifying manufacturing defects early, allowing workers to stop production and address problems before vehicles leave the factory.
Toyota also says it applies rigorous quality standards across vehicle development, manufacturing, and its supplier network.
Larger vehicles feature prominently near the top, including the Toyota Sequoia, 4Runner, Tundra, and Tacoma.
The Tundra has a 28.2% estimated chance of reaching 250,000 miles, while the Tacoma comes in at 25.0%.
However, longevity is not limited to trucks and SUVs. The Toyota Avalon ranks eighth at 23.2%, while the Honda Civic makes the list at 15.0%, showing that smaller passenger cars can also perform well.
For buyers considering long-term ownership costs, durability is only part of the equation. Another important factor is depreciation, as shown in our ranking of the cars that hold and lose their value the most.
Six hybrid models appear in the ranking, led by the Lexus RX Hybrid at 28.9% and Toyota Highlander Hybrid at 20.7%.
The Honda Accord Hybrid follows at 18.5%, while the Toyota Avalon Hybrid, Prius, and Camry Hybrid also make the list.
More broadly, Toyota, Lexus, Honda, and Acura collectively account for 25 of the 27 ranked vehicles. The only exceptions are the Mercedes-Benz G-Class at 17.3% and Chevrolet Suburban at 11.6%, highlighting how heavily this ranking favors Japanese automakers.

This reflects the luxury-heavy mix of European brands in the U.S. market. Six of the eight European brands listed average more than $61,000, with MINI ($41,075) and Volkswagen ($40,185) as the exceptions.
These higher averages largely reflect the types of vehicles European brands sell in America, rather than a direct price comparison between equivalent models.
Japanese and South Korean brands account for seven of the eight automakers averaging below $40,000. Toyota sits just above that group at $44,168, nearly $7,000 below the industry average.
Many Asian automakers sell their upscale vehicles under separate badges, including Lexus, Acura, Genesis, and Infiniti. Their mainstream brands continue to offer smaller cars and crossovers, helping keep average transaction prices lower.

Buick is the only American brand averaging below $40,000, at $37,400. Although its lineup consists entirely of SUVs, it lacks the full-size pickups that lift averages at Ford, Chevrolet, and GMC.
Overall, the ranking highlights how vehicle mix, rather than brand prestige alone, shapes what Americans pay for new cars.

articles.title_orig: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
articles.title_zh: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
articles.content_orig:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents , starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms .
AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf , have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.
Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch , comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.
Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns , pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.
It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.
As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.
The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim , an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.
Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali , a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.
“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”
Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian , a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.
He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.
Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame ? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.
Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.
Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times . Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.
Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.
Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

articles.title_orig: Has the AI Bubble Already Burst?
articles.title_zh: Has the AI Bubble Already Burst?
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Although the AI industry has been the darling of Wall Street for years, the sector now makes investors wince as it reckons with a wave of concerns over dizzying spending and its promise to make the technology profitable.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index was indicative of this shift after plummeting 5.28 percent on Friday, wiping out all gains it had recorded since the start of the year.
"Markets were euphoric" about AI but "there's a huge repricing going on right now," Steve Sostick, a financial analyst with Interactive Brokers, told AFP.
The so-called "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks largely driving the market -- Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta and Tesla -- have seen their combined market capitalization fall by more than $4 trillion in the past month-and-a-half, according to an AFP analysis based on Bloomberg data -- a decrease larger than the annual GDP of France.
"You have a situation now where the bubble already deflated...The question now is how far down will it go?" Adam Sarhan, head of the financial platform MarketTerminal.com, told AFP in an interview.
- US midterms and Nvidia controversy -
While the trajectory of stock markets is never linear, the setbacks have piled up on tech darlings this month.
First, US midterm elections dominated by Democrats "really turned the tide, as it told us that American voters are not fans of artificial intelligence," Sostick said, referencing the many local ballot box measures restricting data centers.
Second, the biggest company in the semiconductor industry, Nvidia, has seen its longtime chief Jensen Huang resign over multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funneled restricted chips to that country.
With the chip market being so key to the AI industry, the disruption has had widespread ripple effects in the stock market.
"The AI investment boom has gone from a promising technology story to a capital markets extravaganza," said Stephen Innes, a manager at SPI Asset Management, with billions of dollars spent to develop the technology.
But as spending has ballooned, so has debt -- and profits have yet to match.
"As the capital needs grew, we started to see investors question how profitable all these investments might be, whether all this money was being spent wisely...the market hadn't been really asking these questions before," Sostick said.
"It seems absurd to ask people to invest money and not have a real sense of what's going to be the return on that investment," he added.
AI giant Anthropic, maker of Claude AI software, made its stock market debut Thursday, raking in an eye-watering $91 billion.
However, even with such a windfall, the company has acknowledged that its financing needs could require it to borrow money in the future.
"The opaqueness of AI-related debt is further compounded by circular links in the form of mutual commitments and interlinked ownerships between firms in the AI supply chain," the European Central Bank warned in a recent report.

articles.title_orig: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.title_zh: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.content_orig:
Pain, swelling, and stiffness in the knees can be downright debilitating.
As cartilage breaks down in these joints, it can significantly reduce freedom of movement and cause pain, even when standing still or sitting.
Surprisingly enough, core exercises may be a neglected form of treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
A randomized controlled trial in India has now found that working out the abdominal muscles may have a trickle-down effect for the knees.
Strengthening the abdomen won't stop cartilage from degenerating, but in this particular trial, when core exercises were added to typical rehabilitation programs, it improved physical function more than conventional exercises alone.
What's more, patients who did the core exercises also reported significantly less pain when moving about.
The findings are published in Scientific Reports , and while the study is small, the methodology was rigorously designed.
The trial involved 100 participants, aged 40 to 80, with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis.
Roughly half the group were randomized to partake in conventional knee-focused rehabilitation for 12 weeks.
During the trial, this half of the group partook in 45 minutes of supervised exercise three times a week for four weeks.
Each session involved progressive strengthening, range-of-motion, and functional exercises, such as straight-leg raises and moves to strengthen the quadriceps.
Participants then continued these exercises at home on their own for an additional 8 weeks.
Meanwhile, the other half of the group was randomized to undertake a different rehabilitation program.
This one involved a mix of conventional knee-based rehabilitation exercises and progressive core-targeting exercises.
The core exercises included abdominal bracing, glute bridges, forearm planks, arm raises while lying down, heel taps, and alternating arm-and-leg movements similar to dead bugs.
After the 12-week intervention period, both groups demonstrated significant reductions in resting pain.
But it was the group that also partook in core training that demonstrated greater improvements in physical function tests and reported less pain when moving about.
Importantly, this group also reported greater improvements in their quality of life.
The authors of the study don't know why core training led to these benefits, but they suggest that an improvement in posture control may help stabilize the body's core during exercise, putting less strain on the lower limbs.
"Collectively," the team concludes , "these biomechanical adaptations provide a plausible explanation for the greater improvement observed in pain, physical function, and quality of life compared with conventional knee-focused strengthening alone."
The findings are supported by previous research, which also suggests that the core is a neglected part of knee pain.
In 2021, for instance, a peer-reviewed narrative review argued that despite preliminary findings that core training is beneficial for knee issues, more research is needed.
"Investigations that show it is safe and effective in older adults have not been adapted to/incorporated into treatment recommendations for those with knee osteoarthritis," the authors argued.
This year, the results of several randomized clinical trials have begun to roll in.
One trial among 48 patients with knee osteoarthritis in Pakistan, for example, also found that adding core stability training to knee exercises produced greater improvements in pain, knee mobility, and quality of life after 12 weeks.
Plus, a larger study of 100 patients found that adding core exercises to conventional knee rehabilitation was more effective than adding foot-and-ankle strengthening.
That seemed to be particularly true for outcomes like pain and physical function.
Related: Study of 33,500 CT Scans Challenges a Common Assumption About Ab Strength And Back Pain
These randomized trials are small, but their findings suggest that exclusively targeting the joints during osteoarthritis treatment may not be the best move.
The whole body is connected, and the function of our extremities is founded upon the stability of our trunk.
Ab exercises may help cut to the core of the issue.
The research has been published in Scientific Reports .

Baby boomers have transformed every demographic they aged into. Now they are trying to redefine old age .
This year, the oldest boomers are turning 80 and the youngest ones will be eligible to claim Social Security . They are living longer. They are more educated than prior generations and many of them are well-off.
This group of 76 million babies born between 1946 and 1964 is a massive generation. They grew up in an era of post-World War II prosperity and upward mobility, against the backdrop of the Civil Rights Era and President John F. Kennedy’s assassination. articles.title_orig: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.title_zh: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.content_orig:
Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument
The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons appears to outpace efforts to regulate them.
The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.
Despite mounting pressure, an agreement to discuss an instrument to regulate autonomous weapons over the next two years fell short of the urgent action rights groups said was needed to address the looming threat.
“We’re starting to see artificial intelligence … being fielded in the battlefield and perhaps also already in weapon systems. If we leave this unregulated, it will be much more difficult to put the genie back in the bottle,” said Dr Cordula Droege, the director of international law, movement and partnerships at the ICRC.
Autonomous weapons are military systems that act without human supervision, often through the use of artificial intelligence or other forms of robotics.
As artificial intelligence has grown exponentially in recent years, militaries and manufacturers have created increasingly advanced weapons systems for both offensive and defensive purposes.
These systems include the use of AI in generating target banks , as was done by the Israeli military in Gaza, as well as semi-autonomous drones in the Ukraine-Russia war, which have “last-mile capability”, where AI takes over in the drone’s final approach to its target.
The president of the ICRC, Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, and the UN secretary general, António Guterres, have called for a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions on use of weapons. In particular, the ICRC has called for a ban on the use of autonomous weapons against personnel, as well as ensuring that weapons systems behave predictably and placing limits on weapons including restricting their use to military objectives.
Experts have said that given the rapid development of autonomous weapons and AI, the failure to create adequate regulations could have dangerous repercussions.
“It’s not about banning all autonomous weapon systems, but to set limits in an international treaty of red lines that should never be crossed,” said Droege. “We’re very close to crossing those red lines, particularly targeting human beings through machines should be a moral red line.”
Other rights groups warned that any delay towards regulation of these weapons risked allowing private industry and militaries to set the norms of how autonomous weapons are used.
Already, autonomous weapons have led to civilian harm. Three civilians were killed by a Russian drone guided by an AI system in July in Zaporizhzhia in south-eastern Ukraine. The drone tried to hit a petrol station, probably its intended target, but instead crashed into a wall, killing three people in a fountain of shrapnel.
In Gaza, Israel has used AI-assisted targeting methods to fill its target banks much faster than humanly possible since the start of the war. As a result, rights groups have said that civilians and people with tenuous links to militant groups were erroneously killed.
In Iran, a US strike that hit an elementary school, killing 156 civilians including 120 schoolchildren, reportedly was a result of faulty intelligence gathered by AI systems.
Anna Hehir, the head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, said further delay to a strong treaty could see “more cases of mass civilian harm that we’ve seen over the past 18 months to two years”, warning that some of these mass casualty events could dwarf what has already occurred. She said manufacturers and militaries were trying to develop “swarm” capabilities, where hundreds or thousands of autonomous drones act at the same time.
“This has the potential for high damage, just because of the sheer mass of systems that would be autonomous. All it takes is for one of them to face algorithmic error and then the entire swarm is utilised and led down a path based on that error … particularly if they’re programmed to target humans.”
There is also a risk of proliferation, as non-state groups increasingly use AI to program their weapons systems, as was the case when the Houthi movement in Yemen used Claude to “vibe code” ballistic missiles.
Armed Islamist groups in Africa’s Sahel region have reportedly used AI tools to improve drone ballistics and for operational planning.
“This is the only thing that is important this week. It’s not really the substance of laws. What’s on the agenda here, after 13 years, is the political will finally present to start to get serious about regulation of autonomous weapons systems,” said a senior diplomat with knowledge of the UN discussions.

articles.title_orig: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?
articles.title_zh: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?
articles.content_orig:
Every month, more than 12,000 applications are made to Social Security Scotland for disability support.
The number of Scots receiving these benefits has risen sharply since the Covid pandemic, and is projected to hit one million by the end of the decade.
This has been driven in part by younger people and claims for mental health conditions.
The cost of the system has been growing, posing additional challenges for Scottish ministers facing a tight budget settlement.
But with the UK government considering a radical redesign of support in England and Wales, they insist that Scotland's welfare state does not need to be trimmed.
Why has there been such an increase in claims in Scotland, and can the government afford to continue its more generous approach?
Scotland has long had a higher rate of ill health among adults than other parts of the UK, often attributed to its history of heavy industry and relatively high levels of poverty in certain areas.
But the change seen in recent years has different roots.
There has been a notable uptick in disability across the UK since the Covid pandemic - and it is most pronounced north of the border.
The percentage of Scotland's working-age population, aged 16 to 64, reporting having a disability increased from 19% in 2020-21 to 28% in 2023-24 .
In children aged under 16, it doubled from 6% to 12%.
That has translated into a rising number of people receiving disability benefits - in total there are about 800,000 people in receipt of them today.
The Scottish Fiscal Commission says there has been a "shift in the age profile of applicants" since 2020.
Some 35% of the new applicants for Adult Disability Payment , since it was rolled out as Scotland's main disability benefit in 2022, have been people under 35. Over half are under 45.
Mental health is a key element in this, with 41% of the ADP caseload concerning "mental and behavioural disorders".
Almost half of those are "neurotic and stress related" conditions, such as anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.
If you look back before social security was devolved to Holyrood, mental and behavioural disorders accounted for only 26% of the claims for Personal Independence Payments, the main disability payment in the UK system.
Among children, these conditions now account for 64% of applications in Scotland - with the number of people under 16 receiving the Child Disability Payment for them more than doubling from 30,000 in 2020 to 75,000 this year.
Meanwhile, mental health conditions play a much smaller role in benefit claims from older people, accounting for 13% of the Pension Age Disability Payment caseload - behind both back and joint issues and diseases of the circulatory system.
There are inevitably some who characterise it as the product of an overly sensitive "snowflake generation".
But others note that the current cohort of young people spent their formative years in lockdown before emerging into a cost-of-living crisis and the destabilising rise of AI - with polling suggesting that the majority believe they will be worse off than their parents .
Mental health charity Scottish Action for Mental Health (SAMH) says young people today are "growing up significantly more mentally distressed".
Chief executive Billy Watson said they face a "relentless" pace of life, with social media constantly exposing them to unsettling news and world events and unrealistic social comparison.
Data published this week from the Scottish Health Survey suggested that mental wellbeing - measured using an internationally-recognised scoring system - had recovered to pre-pandemic levels.
However, the 16 to 24 age group had the lowest score of any included, and around a quarter of young adults reported poor enough mental health to suggest a possible psychiatric disorder.
An independent review for the UK government by Prof Peter Fonagy last month said the problems faced by young people were real , with dramatically increasing cases of mental distress including depression and anxiety.
But Fonagy also warned of an "increasing risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis".
He said this was because "diagnosis has become the primary gateway to support that could and should be available earlier".
This was echoed by Alan Milburn, author of the UK government's review of support for young people in England and Wales.
He said that "in too many places, diagnosis has inappropriately become the key that unlocks help", which has "created pressure on people to seek a diagnosis".
As an aside, it should be noted that while Milburn's review centred on employment prospects, benefit uptake does not always read across directly to this; Adult Disability Payment is not an "out of work" benefit like Jobseeker's Allowance.
The employment rate among disabled people in Scotland is more than 50%, and on the flip side studies have suggested that almost half of those not in education, employment or training are not claiming benefits either.
Milburn's review proposed sweeping changes to the youth support network in England and Wales, including faster access to mental health services and a complete replacement of Personal Independence Payments.
But in Scotland, "Pip" has already been replaced by Adult Disability Payment.
There was a very deliberate wave of publicity around the launch of the new benefit in 2022 - alongside the versions for children and pensioners - in a bid to increase uptake among people who might have been entitled to the likes of Pip, but never claimed.
With more money being spent on the Scottish system - it costs about £1bn a year over and above the block grant from Westminster - there is an easy narrative that it is inherently more generous.
A report last year concluded that it was more " significantly more compassionate " and "kinder in tone and approach".
However, it is worth noting that more than half of initial applications for ADP have been rejected, with 43% approved compared with 54% denied - broadly in line with the system in England and Wales.
There has been a steady increase in rejections since ADP was rolled out in 2022 - in the first few months only a quarter of applications were rejected, but over the past year it has been 67%.
Asked about this, Education Secretary Mairi McAllan said Social Security Scotland undertook a "very robust and close examination of all applications", and that people had to prove they were in need.
Last year also saw a record number of referrals rejected from NHS child mental health services , with ministers saying specialist services are only right for a small proportion of young people.
Even with an increase in rejections, the overall number of claims and the cost of the devolved social security system has been rising - and ADP alone makes up more than half of the total cost.
The last forecast from the SFC was for the social security bill to be £7.8bn in 2027-28 - within that, ADP accounts for £4.2bn, the pension-age disability payment £972m and child disability payment £659m.
By 2030-31, the cost is forecast to rise to £9.2bn - which has prompted questions from auditors and opposition parties alike about whether it is sustainable.
Ministers have repeatedly insisted that they view benefits as an investment in the people of Scotland.
But they have also said they will look carefully at Milburn's proposals.
A more generous system is not necessarily an easy choice, when it entails higher rates of income tax and cuts to other budgets.
There is also the possibility that changes down south could widen the existing £1bn funding gap, by cutting welfare spending at Westminster.
First Minister John Swinney has suggested that there are "potentially some significant financial implications that could be negative" for Holyrood.
But if money cut from benefits ends up being spent on education or local employment services - devolved issues - it would end up flowing back into the Scottish budget regardless.

articles.title_orig: What to know about US-China competition as Trump and Xi meet again this week - Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.title_zh: What to know about US-China competition as Trump and Xi meet again this week - Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.source: Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes.
As they dispersed to their capitals, the presidents had few tangible gains to show for a summit hastily assembled in a matter of weeks, bypassing the months of groundwork that typically underpin diplomatic breakthroughs.
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking, a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to journalists.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
But if any substantive understandings were reached behind closed doors, none of them were released to the public.
The summit’s pageantry fit a familiar pattern for Trump, who has repeatedly staged headline-grabbing encounters with controversial leaders only to walk away empty-handed. Three high-stakes meetings with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term failed to meaningfully shift relations between Washington and Pyongyang, and a meeting with Putin in Anchorage last year likewise failed to generate progress toward ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.
This time, the spectacular gathering lasted just an hour and a half, and produced only a readout of four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically, overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against the Islamic Republic this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the start of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that [Putin] and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since their summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in the Republican president’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with  Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.
